claims.text: Pennsylvania ballots will be rejected without outer and inner envelopes.
claims.reasoning: Multiple high‑reputation sources (NPR, Pennsylvania government site) state that state law requires both an outer declaration envelope and an inner secrecy envelope, and that ballots lacking either are rejected. Additional reputable reports (Lawfare, Business Insider) confirm the Supreme Court ruling that ballots without the inner envelope are rejected, reinforcing the claim.
caveats: The requirement applies only to ballots returned on time and under current Pennsylvania law; proposed legislative changes have not been enacted.
Rejection depends on the specific error (missing date/signature on outer envelope or missing inner secrecy envelope).
Some counties may allow voters to correct certain errors with a provisional ballot.

claims.text: The FBI is in possession of the president of the US's son  Hunter Biden's laptop.
claims.reasoning: Multiple high‑reputation sources (judiciary.house.gov, Wikipedia, congress.gov, and a Senate office) explicitly state that the FBI seized and retained Hunter Biden's laptop or its hard drive, confirming the claim.
caveats: The statements refer to the FBI's custody of the laptop's hard drive or the seized device as of December 2019 and June 2024; they do not address any later disposition.
Some sources describe the laptop as "abandoned" or provided by a third‑party repairer, which may affect interpretations of ownership.

claims.text: Melissa Francis is married to Wray Thorn.
claims.reasoning: All provided sources state that Melissa Francis is married to Wray Thorn, including a high‑reputation Wikipedia entry and several medium‑reputation outlets. No source contradicts the claim. The only minor discrepancy is the reported marriage year (1997 vs 1999), which does not affect the fact of the marriage.
caveats: Sources differ on the exact year of marriage (1997 vs 1999), but all agree the couple is married.

claims.text: U.S. President Donald Trump and his wife, First Lady Melania Trump, have tested positive for COVID-19
claims.reasoning: Multiple high‑reputation sources (NPR, BBC, FactCheck.org) report that President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump announced they tested positive for COVID‑19 in October 2020, and a YouTube news segment corroborates this. An earlier CNN article notes a negative test for Melania in March 2020, but that refers to a different time and does not negate the later positive result.
caveats: The CNN report refers to a March 2020 test that was negative; the positive test occurred later, in October 2020.
The claim is about at least one instance of a positive test, not a continuous status.

claims.text: The iPhone 12 won’t come with earphones and a charging adapter.
claims.reasoning: Three reputable sources (CNBC, Business Insider, and Apple support) explicitly state that the iPhone 12 box does not include EarPods or a power adapter, confirming the claim. Two low‑reputation rumor sites contradict the claim, but their credibility is far lower than the supporting sources.
caveats: The claim refers to the contents of the standard retail box; accessories can be purchased separately.

claims.reasoning: Multiple high‑reputation sources (Wikipedia, World Bank, WTO) confirm that Ngozi Okonjo‑Iweala of Nigeria was appointed Director‑General of the WTO in February 2021 and is the first woman (and first African) to hold the position.

claims.text: Officer who wore Trump 2020 mask to polls to face disciplinary action
claims.reasoning: Multiple reputable sources (AP News, CBS News, NBC News, NBC Miami) report that a Miami police officer was photographed wearing a "Trump 2020" mask at an early voting site and that the officer is facing disciplinary action, confirming the claim.
caveats: The officer's name was not officially confirmed by the police department, though the badge identified him as Officer Ubeda.
It was not definitively stated whether the officer was on duty at the time, but disciplinary action is still being considered.

claims.reasoning: All provided reputable sources (BBC, NPR, FactCheck.org, CNBC, and WEF) report that President Trump directed a halt to U.S. funding for the WHO pending a review of the agency's handling of the coronavirus, directly matching the claim.

claims.text: The White House blocked a plan to send facemasks to every household in April 2020.
claims.reasoning: Multiple reputable sources (Wikipedia and CNBC) report that the White House abandoned a plan to distribute reusable masks to every U.S. household in April 2020, and additional news outlets (NBC News, Poynter, Business Insider) corroborate this. No evidence contradicts the claim.
caveats: The term "blocked" is interpreted as the White House deciding to scrap or abandon the plan, as described by the sources.
The masks were later distributed through other channels (nonprofits, agencies) rather than direct household mailing.

claims.text: You could text RBG to 50409 to sign a petition to tell your senator not to replace Ruth Bader Ginsberg in the Supreme court until after the 2020 election

caveats: The Resistbot service was active in September 2020; its current availability may have changed.

The claim is qualified by the district continuing COVID‑19 safety protocols.
